subtype: Dropping a hobby to fit in [Actor]
passage:
September: Elizabeth practised violin every evening in the church hall and loved the solo she'd been given for Christmas. At lunch, Anjali and the girls from the new group laughed: "Violin? That's so aunty." Elizabeth laughed along.
October: She told Sister Mary she was too busy with studies to play at Christmas. She spent evenings at Anjali's house instead, scrolling videos with the group. She felt included. Mostly.
December: At the Christmas service, a younger girl played Elizabeth's solo, a bit shakily. Elizabeth sat in the back pew with her friends, whispering. When the last note ended, her throat went tight, and she didn't know why she wanted to cry.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth tell Sister Mary in October?
qa.a: She told Sister Mary she was too busy with studies to play at Christmas.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth's throat go tight when the last note ended?
qa.a: Hearing someone else play her solo brought back how much she loved the violin, and she felt the loss she had traded for fitting in.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do now that she has felt the loss?
qa.a: She could quietly ask Sister Mary if she can return to practice, and stay close to friends who accept the violin as part of her.

qa.q: How might Anjali and the group see the violin, compared with Elizabeth?
qa.a: To them it's just 'aunty' and uncool, a joke, while for Elizabeth it was something she loved and gave up to belong.

grounding: Over a term, a teenager drops the violin because her new group finds it uncool and later feels the loss.

subtype: Dropping a hobby to fit in [Actor]
passage: Akash, you're thinking of quitting chess because your friends tease you? Come, let your Aparna mami tell you something. At fifteen, I was the best chess player in our school in Nagpur. I played every evening with my father on the verandah. Then I started sitting with a new group of girls who thought chess was for "boring nerds". One day one of them saw my chess book and laughed so loudly the whole bench turned. The next week I told my father I was tired of chess. He looked at me for a long time and put the board away. I felt light, accepted. It was only years later, when he was gone and I found that board in the cupboard, that I understood what I'd given up. Play if you love it, beta.

qa.q: What did Aparna tell her father the week after the girl laughed?
qa.a: She told her father she was tired of chess.

qa.q: Why did Aparna feel light and accepted after quitting?
qa.a: Dropping chess helped her fit in with the new group, and at fifteen belonging felt more urgent than the game she loved.

qa.q: What choice is Aparna mami hoping Akash will make?
qa.a: She hopes Akash keeps playing if the love is real, instead of dropping it for friends' approval and feeling the loss later.

qa.q: How might Aparna's father have felt when he put the board away?
qa.a: He may have felt quietly sad, losing the evenings on the verandah with his daughter, though he let her choose.

grounding: An aunt recalls quitting chess at fifteen to fit in with a group and only later feeling what she had lost.

subtype: Dropping a hobby to fit in [Actor]
passage: The bhajan group's practice was at five, and the bus to the temple came only once an hour. At 4:40 Suraj stood at the stop, harmonium book in his bag, when Wasim and the others rode up on their cycles. "Where are you going, uncle-ji?" Wasim grinned. "Singing with the uncles again?" The others laughed. "Come to the ground. Match against the Sector 9 boys." Suraj looked at the empty road, the bus nowhere in sight, his friends waiting. He shoved the book deeper into his bag. "Just going home," he said, and climbed on behind Wasim. He didn't go back to practice that month, or the next. In April, passing the temple, he heard the group singing the song he used to lead, and walked faster.

qa.q: What was in Suraj's bag at the bus stop?
qa.a: His harmonium book.

qa.q: Why did Suraj shove the book deeper into his bag?
qa.a: He didn't want Wasim and the others to see it; fitting in with them felt more urgent than the singing he loved.

qa.q: At what moment could Suraj have chosen differently, and how?
qa.a: At the bus stop he could have said, 'Practice first, I'll come after,' keeping both his friends and the bhajan group.

qa.q: How might the bhajan group feel about Suraj's absence?
qa.a: They may miss the voice that used to lead their song and wonder why he stopped coming.

grounding: With the bus late and friends teasing, a teenager abandons bhajan singing to fit in, and feels the loss months later.

subtype: Dropping a hobby to fit in [Actor]
passage:
Rekha had done Kathak since she was six, every Tuesday and Friday at the dance school above the sweet shop in Lucknow. Then, in Class 9, she moved into Charu's group. Charu's group went to the mall after school, knew all the new songs and called classical dance 'so aunty'.
When Charu saw the ghungroo in Rekha's bag, she laughed. 'You still do that? Cute.'
The next week Rekha told her guru she had too much homework. She put the ghungroo in the steel trunk under her bed.
For months it felt fine. Mall, songs, Charu's jokes.
Then in December, walking past the sweet shop, she heard the tabla upstairs and the tatkar of small feet. She stood on the pavement until the piece ended, her chest aching, and couldn't explain to Charu why she had gone so quiet.

qa.q: Where did Rekha put her ghungroo?
qa.a: In the steel trunk under her bed.

qa.q: Why did Rekha give up Kathak after Charu's laugh?
qa.a: Belonging to Charu's group mattered so much that looking 'aunty' felt like a risk; giving up dance seemed a small price to fit in.

qa.q: What was the turning point in December, and what could Rekha choose now?
qa.a: Hearing the tabla above the sweet shop and feeling her chest ache; Rekha could return to class, even one day a week, and decide what she loves without waiting for Charu's verdict.

qa.q: How might Charu see Rekha's sudden quietness on the pavement?
qa.a: Charu probably has no idea why; her 'Cute' was a throwaway laugh, and she may not realise it cost Rekha something she loved.

grounding: A teenager quits a much-loved dance class because her new group finds it uncool, and feels the loss months later.

subtype: Dropping a hobby to fit in [Actor]
passage:
'Vikas, your binoculars are in the dustbin.' Deepak held them up. 'These were your birthday present.'
'Keep them if you want, bhaiya. I'm done with birds.'
'Since when? Last month you woke me at five to see a kingfisher.'
'Since the class found out. Nitin's gang calls me Bird Uncle now. In the group they sent a video of a pigeon with my face on it.'
Deepak sat on the bed. 'So you're quitting because of Nitin.'
'I'm quitting because it's embarrassing. Nobody normal does it.'
'You loved it, though.'
Vikas looked at the window, where a bulbul was hopping on the grill. Vikas watched it a second too long, then turned away. 'Doesn't matter.'
Deepak put the binoculars quietly on the top shelf, not in the bin.

qa.q: What did the class group send about Vikas?
qa.a: A video of a pigeon with Vikas's face on it.

qa.q: What does Vikas watching the bulbul 'a second too long' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Vikas still loves birds; quitting to escape the teasing is covering a real interest that hasn't gone away.

qa.q: What choice did Deepak make at the end, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Putting the binoculars on the top shelf instead of in the bin; it respects Vikas's decision for now but keeps the door open for when the loss is felt.

qa.q: How does Deepak see Vikas's decision?
qa.a: Deepak remembers being woken at five for a kingfisher, so he sees a real love being given up because of Nitin's gang, not because Vikas stopped caring.

grounding: A teenager throws away birding binoculars because classmates mock the hobby, while an older brother sees the interest is still there.
